Simpler regulatory frameworks are inherently superior to complex ones.

The Wall Street Journal has also analyzed access to data and performed similar assessments.
Gainful employment regulations, as written, apply only to for-profit schools and specific certificate programs.

assumptions.text: Audiences value transparency and equity in educational accountability systems.
Public trust in higher education depends on measurable outcomes and fairness in oversight.
Data availability is a sufficient condition for implementing equitable policy reforms.
Congressional intent can be inferred from legislative context and historical participation, even when not explicitly stated.
Policymakers should act based on broader public interests rather than narrow institutional protection.
Research that reveals systemic inequities in accountability is inherently valuable and socially beneficial.
The speaker’s personal involvement in past legislation grants them legitimate authority to interpret congressional intent.
For-profit schools have historically received disproportionate scrutiny compared to their actual contribution to student failure rates.
Extending accountability to all sectors will improve student protection and institutional quality.
The media and academic communities recognize the importance of empirical evidence over rhetorical claims in policy debates.

The other thing that I think really should happen is basically this kind of shift to program mobile accountability.

explicit_propositions.text: The College Scorecard provides program-level data on earnings and debt outcomes.
Students with excessive debt face unaffordable financial burdens regardless of their institution's tax status.
Future discussions should center on program-level outcome data.
Program-level outcome data should revolutionize accountability in higher education.
The distinction between for-profit and nonprofit institutions does not affect the severity of a student’s debt burden.
There will be increased attention on program-level data due to its availability.
Current debates about punishing for-profits or subsidizing publics are outdated.
TPPF has developed a 'dead as a percent of earnings' metric to assess debt risk.
A 'time to repayment' metric is useful for evaluating educational investment.
Preston Cooper has proposed a return-on-investment (ROI) measure for programs.

assumptions.text: Accountability in higher education should be based on measurable economic outcomes rather than institutional type.
Students prioritize long-term financial outcomes when choosing educational programs.
Available data on earnings and debt is reliable enough to inform policy decisions.
Policy makers and educators are currently underutilizing existing program-level data.
Public understanding of educational value would improve with transparent, simple-to-understand metrics.
Institutional tax status (e.g., for-profit vs. nonprofit) is irrelevant to individual student financial well-being after graduation.
The current system of higher education accountability fails students by ignoring post-graduation outcomes.
Simple, standardized metrics promote fairer and more effective evaluation of programs.
Stakeholders including policymakers, schools, and students trust data-driven approaches over ideological debates.
Shifts toward program-level accountability are feasible and likely to gain traction with sufficient evidence.
